items.definition: Damage caused by insiders, on purpose or by mistake, including theft and unauthorised software.
items.examples: Copying the customer database to a USB before resigning; installing pirated software.
items.examTip: Insiders have legitimate access, so they are harder to detect. Say WHO did WHAT.
keyFacts: Theft of equipment, data or licences
Unauthorised software brings legal and malware risks

items.definition: Physical events, natural, accidental or deliberate, that damage IT systems and data.
items.examples: A burst pipe flooding a server room; arson; a power cut.
items.examTip: Justifies off-site backups and disaster recovery plans.
keyFacts: Destroys hardware and the data on it
Reduce with off-site backups, UPS, fire suppression

items.definition: Poor habits and weak controls that make an organisation easier to attack.
items.examples: An unlocked server room; unescorted visitors; staff on dodgy download sites.
items.examTip: A human weakness: fix it with training and policy, not just technology.

items.term: Accidental Loss/Disclosure of Data or Credentials
items.definition: Data or logins exposed through human error rather than a deliberate attack.
items.examples: Emailing customer data to the wrong person; a password on a sticky note.
items.examTip: Root causes: negligence, poor training, not following procedures.

items.definition: Malicious code that attaches to a file and copies itself when the file is run.
items.examples: A macro virus in a Word document.
items.examTip: Know the types: boot sector, web script, macro, worm, rootkit, trojan, browser hijack, polymorphic.
keyFacts: Worm: spreads across networks by itself
Rootkit: hides deep in the OS
Polymorphic: changes its code to avoid detection

items.definition: Software that secretly collects information about a user and sends it to a third party.
items.examples: A keylogger recording passwords.
items.examTip: Keylogger = records keystrokes to steal logins. A favourite exam term.

items.definition: Software that displays or downloads adverts, from legitimate to deceptive.
items.examples: A free app showing pop-ups; unwanted software bundled with a download.
items.examTip: Not all adware is illegal: tell legitimate adware from abusive adware.
keyFacts: Legitimate adware funds free apps with consent

items.definition: Malware that locks or encrypts your data and demands payment to restore it.
items.examples: An encryptor scrambling all company files.
items.examTip: Best defence: tested OFFLINE backups, so you can restore without paying.
keyFacts: Defend with offline backups, patching, training

items.definition: Infected devices controlled remotely; many together form a botnet.
items.examples: Thousands of infected IoT devices flooding a website.
items.examTip: Botnets link malware to DDoS attacks: a common exam link.

items.definition: Gaining unauthorised access to systems or data.
items.examples: A DDoS taking a website offline; changing records in a database.
items.examTip: DoS = one source; DDoS = many (a botnet).
keyFacts: DoS: one machine floods a target

items.definition: Deliberately damaging or corrupting data, systems or infrastructure.
items.examples: Poisoning AI training data; hijacking connected machinery.
items.examTip: "Fakes" includes AI-generated images, video and audio.

items.definition: Tricking people into giving away secure information instead of attacking technology.
items.examples: A fake bank email; a call pretending to be IT support.
items.examTip: Know the variants: phishing, vishing, smishing, whaling, spear phishing.
keyFacts: Whaling: senior staff; spear phishing: one person

items.definition: Threats that involve physically reaching a secure area or device.
items.examples: Tailgating through a door; shoulder surfing a password.
items.examTip: Tailgating = following someone through a secure door. Learn this definition.
keyFacts: Area access: tailgating, forced entry, impersonation
Device access: unattended devices, shoulder surfing, theft
Devices in public places are most exposed

items.definition: The organisation can't operate or deliver its products and services.
items.examples: A production line stopped by ransomware; a website down so no orders.
items.examTip: Operational = the business can't function.

items.definition: The money an incident costs: lost income, compensation and legal costs.
items.examples: GDPR fines; refunds to affected customers.
items.examTip: Split it into organisational costs, compensation and legal liability.

items.definition: Damage to how customers and the public see the organisation.
items.examples: Angry reviews on social media after a breach.
items.examTip: Often the longest-lasting impact: lost trust is hard to rebuild.

items.definition: Theft or exposure of an organisation's valuable ideas and secrets.
items.examples: A rival stealing a new product design.
items.examTip: Destroys competitive advantage even with no personal data involved.

items.definition: The National Cyber Security Centre: the UK authority publishing threat reports and advice.
items.examples: Checking the NCSC site for the latest ransomware advisory.
items.examTip: NCSC = UK. Use it because threats keep changing.

items.definition: The US National Institute of Standards and Technology, which issues security standards and advisories.
items.examples: Following NIST guidance on password policy.
items.examTip: NIST = the US equivalent of the NCSC.

items.definition: A non-profit whose Top 10 lists the most critical web application security risks.
items.examples: Checking a website for SQL injection using the OWASP Top 10.
items.examTip: Used in penetration testing: link the two.

items.definition: Weaknesses in network set-up, especially open firewall ports and external storage.
items.examples: An exposed open port; malware arriving on a USB stick.
items.examTip: Port types: well-known (e.g. 80 for HTTP), registered, dynamic/private. Open ports = risk.
keyFacts: External storage can bring in malware

items.definition: Weaknesses in how permissions, passwords and accounts are managed.
items.examples: Everyone having admin rights; not disabling a leaver's account.
items.examTip: Password policy points (length, characters, reuse, age) are easy marks.
keyFacts: Password policy: length, characters, reuse, age

items.definition: Weaknesses from untrustworthy, outdated or badly made software.
items.examples: Pirated software with a backdoor; an unpatched web app open to SQL injection.
items.examTip: Zero-day = a new flaw with no patch yet.
keyFacts: Safe downloads: trusted source, HTTPS, malware scan, hash check

items.definition: Weaknesses in the OS and its interfaces, usually from being outdated or misconfigured.
items.examples: An unsupported version of Windows.
items.examTip: Unsupported software no longer gets security patches.

items.definition: Phones depend on their manufacturer (OEM) for updates, so they can be left unpatched.
items.examples: An old Android phone that no longer gets updates.
items.examTip: Updates may be slow or stop entirely, leaving known flaws open.

items.definition: Weaknesses that allow theft of, or physical access to, equipment holding data.
items.examples: A stolen laptop; a badly secured restricted area.
items.examTip: Link to physical security measures.

items.definition: Weaknesses in how people actually use systems day to day.
items.examples: Sharing a login; a process that lets data leave unchecked.
items.examTip: Human weaknesses: fixed by training, policy and better processes.

items.definition: Security risks specific to cloud services and IoT devices.
items.examples: A misconfigured cloud store exposing data; a hijacked IoT camera.
items.examTip: Learn several IoT risks: default passwords, no encryption, no patches, always listening.
keyFacts: Cloud: wrong settings, third-party access, reliance on provider
IoT: weak encryption, default passwords, no patches
IoT: set up by non-IT staff, always listening

items.definition: Where to find up-to-date information on known vulnerabilities.
items.examples: A manufacturer's website; a professional security forum.
items.examTip: Three sources: manufacturer, professional forums, specialist third-party sites.

items.definition: The routes an attacker uses to reach a system.
items.examples: Attacking over Wi-Fi or Bluetooth; exploiting a router.
items.examTip: An attack vector is the "way in".
keyFacts: Wireless: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, NFC, RFID
Internal devices: router, switch, access point

items.definition: Tools that find weaknesses in systems before attackers do.
items.examples: A port scanner; a website vulnerability scanner.
items.examTip: Know the named tools.

items.definition: An outside expert reviewing system designs before they are built.
items.examples: A consultancy reviewing and certifying a new network design.
items.examTip: Shows due diligence and gives independent certification.

items.definition: Authorised simulated attacks to find weak spots, ending in a report.
items.examples: A pen tester trying to break into a network.
items.examTip: Real attack techniques used with permission. Links to OWASP.
keyFacts: Uses a range of attack techniques

items.definition: Managing risk without adding security controls: transfer, avoid or accept it.
items.examples: Buying cyber insurance; stopping a risky activity.
items.examTip: Three options: transfer, avoid, accept.
keyFacts: Transfer: pass it on, e.g. insurance

items.definition: Law protecting personal data and people's privacy rights.
items.examples: Getting consent before collecting data; reporting a breach within 72 hours.
items.examTip: GDPR = personal data and privacy. Don't mix it up with the Computer Misuse Act.
keyFacts: Applies to stored and transferred data
Covers anything that identifies a person

items.definition: Law making unauthorised access to, or modification of, computers and data a crime.
items.examples: Hacking into a system you have no permission to use.
items.examTip: Computer Misuse Act = unauthorised access and modification.
keyFacts: Changing data without permission is an offence

items.definition: The core rules for processing personal data under GDPR.
items.examples: Collecting the minimum data, keeping it accurate, deleting it when done.
items.examTip: Lawful/fair/transparent, set purpose, accurate, minimal, minimum time, secure.

items.definition: The valid legal reasons an organisation can have for processing personal data.
items.examples: Payroll under "contract"; medical data under "vital interest".
items.examTip: Six bases: consent, contract, legitimate interest, vital interest, legal requirement, public interest.

items.definition: The rights people have over their own personal data.
items.examples: Asking for a copy of your data or for it to be deleted.
items.examTip: Access, be informed, correct/erase/restrict, object, portability, no solely automated decisions.
keyFacts: Not subject to solely automated decisions

items.definition: Measures that physically protect equipment, sites and restricted areas.
items.examples: Card entry; fingerprint scanners; CCTV; locked server cabinets.
items.examTip: Group them: locks, card entry, biometrics, surveillance, training.
keyFacts: Card entry: NFC, RFID, QR, chip

items.definition: Copying data so it can be restored after loss, corruption or attack.
items.examples: A weekly full backup plus daily incrementals stored off-site.
items.examTip: Full, incremental (since last backup), differential (since last full). RAID is NOT a backup.
keyFacts: RAID and archiving are not backups
Restore a file, an image or the whole system

items.definition: Software that detects, blocks and removes malware using signatures and heuristics.
items.examples: Quarantining a suspicious file.
items.examTip: Signatures catch known malware; heuristics catch new behaviour.

items.definition: Hardware or software that filters traffic using rules to block unauthorised access.
items.examples: Blocking inbound traffic on every port except those needed.
items.examTip: Inbound and outbound rules; packet filtering; application awareness.

items.definition: Checking users are who they claim to be, often using more than one factor.
items.examples: Password + USB security key; an authenticator app code.
items.examTip: Factors: knowledge, possession, inherence, plus location and behaviour. A USB key = possession.
keyFacts: Tokens: USB key, contactless, code generator

items.definition: Methods that control which users can access which resources.
items.examples: Finance can open accounts but not HR files.
items.examTip: DAC: owners control files. Role-based: by job. Rule-based: rules per user.
keyFacts: DAC: users control their own resources
Applies to apps, files and devices

items.definition: Hardware-based security, e.g. a TPM chip, that adds protection but reduces user control.
items.examples: A TPM checking the system is trusted before start-up.
items.examTip: Benefit: more security. Drawback: less user control and privacy.
keyFacts: Less user control, privacy and anonymity

items.definition: Measures that protect devices and help locate, lock or wipe lost ones.
items.examples: "Find my device"; remotely wiping a stolen phone.
items.examTip: Remote lock/wipe and timed lockout are strong answers.
keyFacts: Screen locks after time or failed logins
Wipe after too many failed attempts

items.definition: Encrypting stored data so a stolen device or drive is unreadable.
items.examples: Full-disk encryption on a laptop.
items.examTip: Protects data "at rest": vital for lost or stolen devices.
keyFacts: File, folder, disk and device encryption

items.definition: Encrypting data in transit so it can't be read if intercepted.
items.examples: HTTPS; VPNs; end-to-end encrypted messaging.
items.examTip: Symmetric = one shared key (AES, fast). Asymmetric = public/private pair (RSA).
keyFacts: Symmetric: one secret key, e.g. AES
Asymmetric: public + private keys, e.g. RSA

items.definition: Precautions that protect a wireless network from unauthorised access.
items.examples: WPA3; hiding the SSID; MAC filtering; changing default passwords.
items.examTip: MAC addresses can be spoofed, so MAC filtering is only medium security.
keyFacts: Change defaults; use VPNs and firewalls

items.definition: Building security in from the start rather than adding it later.
items.examples: Designing with least privilege and assuming attackers will try.
items.examTip: Expect attacks, least privilege, don't rely on secrecy, follow standards (ISO 27000).
